pr_title: Disable automatic write protection on replicas
pr_body:
This allows users to use write protection if they want, but no longer treats it as a catch all. Write protection is not accurate enough to classify all cases correctly. Instead users should configure their replicas to not allow writes and rely on the database erroring if the query is not allowed.


Alternative solution for: https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/42432
Fixes: https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/42432
pr_comments: I am in favor of this. Is there any other reason for rails to know if the db is a replica? If not, I imagine you can remove a fair bit more code.

> Is there any other reason for rails to know if the db is a replica? If not, I imagine you can remove a fair bit more code.

Yes, we need to know a configuration is a replica so that we don't run rake tasks against it. I don't think offhand there is any other code to remove since we're not dropping replica support, just dropping the automatic prevent_writes from it. 

`prevent_writes` was designed for the case where you're sending read queries to your primary and want to make sure they behave similarly to a replica. For example if you're using the auto switcher middleware you dont want your GET requests to have any writes in them (without switching to writing) because when it goes to the replica it won't write. To make GET's going to the primary and replica behave the same, we added this functionality.

Just noticed this line: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/eca7582718225ef40a7618293a13924561194aae/activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_handling.rb#L355. Should it also be removed?  It gets called by `connected_to`; the equivalent line in `connected_to_many` has been removed.
Thanks @ghiculescu that line in connection_handling turned up a lot of places I missed ❤️

issue_context.title: Blank query can't be executed on a readonly database connection
issue_context.body:
Trying to execute a blank SQL query on a readonly (role: :reading) database connection always fails with this error:

```
ActiveRecord::ReadOnlyError: Write query attempted while in readonly mode
```

### Steps to reproduce

```
ActiveRecord::Base.connected_to(role: :reading) { ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute('').count }
ActiveRecord::ReadOnlyError: Write query attempted while in readonly mode:
```

or if you deep dive into why Rails thinks the query can't run on a readonly database:

```
Class.new.extend(ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQL::DatabaseStatements).write_query?('')
=> true
```

### Expected behaviour

The query should be allowed to execute on a readonly connection.
It would return an empty result like when it runs on a read/write connection:

```
ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute('').count
=> 0
```

### Actual behaviour

```
ActiveRecord::Base.connected_to(role: :reading) { ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute('').count }
ActiveRecord::ReadOnlyError: Write query attempted while in readonly mode:
```

### System configuration

**Rails version**: Rails 6.1.3.2
**Ruby version**: ruby 2.7.3p183 (2021-04-05 revision 6847ee089d) [x86_64-darwin20
comments: Thanks for the bug report - https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/42433 should fix this, can you please confirm.

Thanks @ghiculescu for the super fast fix. 

Actually, I forgot one **important** thing: the queries we send are not totally blank. They are suffixed with a comment added by [marginalia](https://github.com/basecamp/marginalia)

Something like:

```
' /*hostname:thehost,application:theapp,controller:index*/'
```

So `sql.blank?` will not be enough

Thanks @dgageot for the issue,

One thing that might help this issue is explaining why you want to run empty queries. I agree it isn't a write query and probably should error that way, but understanding why you want to run empty queries would be helpful for understanding what the best fix might be.

Sure, we have a few cases where we don't query the database though `ActiveRecord`. Instead we use `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute(raw_query)` with a `raw_query` that's computed in a way we don't totally control. It turns out that we hit a bug when switch from `Standby` to rails built-in mechanism.

We tried to fix places where we generate empty queries. All the time, it can early return.
We couldn't fix them all and also we are afraid that future usage of `.execute` could happen with en empty query anyways.

It doesn't seem legit to assume empty queries are write queries since they are essentially no-op so, here I am, opening a ticket :-)

That sounds like a bit of a scary use case, not relevant to this but would love to know how you are protecting against things like SQL injection. 

> It doesn't seem legit to assume empty queries are write queries since they are essentially no-op so, here I am, opening a ticket :-)

Agree! Thanks for raising it.

(I'm working with @dgageot)

We have other cases for which ActiveRecord generates an empty query

```
MyModel.my_scope(list_of_ids).to_sql
```

If `list_of_ids` is empty (which can happen in some use cases), the generated query is `''`

May be our scope is not well written :)
@dgageot @bpaquet would https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/42450 resolve your issue? It looks more generally useful than https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/42433

> If `list_of_ids` is empty (which can happen in some use cases), the generated query is `''`

That is changed in 7.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/42232.
